chunks: "A DMM's sample rate is basically how many readings per second it produces, and it's a trade-off, not a fixed spec. Most DMMs use an integrating ADC.
They average the input over a chosen time, usually a whole number of power-line cycles, called NPLC. At 1 NPLC on 60 hertz mains that's about 16.
7 milliseconds per measurement, so a maximum of about 60 readings a second, less if auto-zero is on. A handheld typically gives 2 to 5 readings a second.
Bench meters let you pick: fast with fewer digits and more noise, or slow, like 10 or 100 NPLC, for the best resolution and noise.

Longer integration does two things: it averages noise down, roughly as one over the square root of the time, and it rejects 50 or 60 hertz interference, because integrating over whole line cycles averages a sine at the line frequency to zero.
Does it matter? For a steady DC rail, a battery voltage, a resistance, no: slow is better. It matters when the signal changes within a reading.
A DMM will average a glitch away, miss a power-up transient, and a signal that varies near the reading rate can even alias, so you see a slow wobble that isn't really there.
For anything fast, I'd use a scope or a faster digitizing mode.
So I choose the reading rate based on the signal: slow for accuracy on stable signals, fast, or a scope, for dynamic ones."
